overview.summary: Architects design buildings and spaces, balancing how they look, how people use them, safety, cost and the surroundings.
overview.problems: They turn a client's needs into plans for homes, schools, offices and public places that are practical and safe to build.
overview.worksWith: Clients, engineers, builders, interior designers, planners and local authorities.
overview.workplaces: Architecture studios, construction companies and government bodies, and building sites during construction.

timeline.title: Plan the day's priorities
timeline.description: The architect checks project deadlines and what each team member needs to finish.
timeline.why: Projects have many stages and approvals with fixed dates.

timeline.title: Designing and drawing
timeline.description: The architect sketches ideas, develops plans in design software and tests layouts, light and how people will move through the building.
timeline.why: Early design decisions shape how people will live and work in a space.

timeline.title: Meeting a client
timeline.description: The architect presents options, listens to feedback and discusses budget and changes.
timeline.why: A building has to serve the people who will use it.

timeline.title: Checking rules and details
timeline.description: The architect checks building regulations, fire and accessibility requirements and coordinates drawings with engineers.
timeline.why: Plans must meet legal and safety standards before anything is built.

timeline.title: Site visit or documents
timeline.description: The architect visits a site to check progress against the drawings, or prepares documents for builders.
timeline.why: What gets built should match what was designed.

timeline.title: Changes and deadlines
timeline.description: Clients change their minds, costs rise and approvals take time, so designs have to adapt.
timeline.why: Few projects go exactly to the first plan.

responsibilities: Understanding what clients and users need
Producing concept designs and detailed drawings
Coordinating with engineers and other specialists
Making sure designs meet building rules
Estimating and managing cost and time
Visiting sites to check the work
challenges: Creative ideas have to be balanced against budgets and regulations.
Designs change often, and rework is common.
Projects can take years from first sketch to finished building.
Qualifying usually takes long study, supervised experience and often a licensing exam.
Pay and working hours vary, and some studios work long hours before deadlines.
workEnvironment: Mostly studio and office work on computers and drawings, with meetings and site visits. The balance depends on the firm and the stage of the project.
rewards: Seeing a building you designed being used
A mix of creativity and practical problem solving
Shaping places where people live and work
tradeoffs: Clients and budgets that limit ideas
Deadlines that can mean long hours
Income and opportunities that vary by country, city and type of firm

activity.title: Draw a floor plan of your own room
steps: Measure the length and width of your room with a tape measure and note the doors and windows.
Draw it on squared paper, using one square for a fixed length such as 50 centimetres.
Sketch a better layout, thinking about movement, light and storage.
Note whether planning a space felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise measuring, drawing to scale and thinking about how people use space.
activity.safety: Do not move heavy furniture alone, and do not climb on anything to take measurements.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
